Pulmonology · published research

Dyspnea

In 28 healthy adults, phototherapy over the stellate-ganglion area reduced perceived dyspnea during inspiratory resistive loading. A small COPD exercise study reported lower exertional dyspnea as a secondary outcome, not a primary dyspnea treatment result.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In 28 healthy adults, phototherapy over the stellate-ganglion area reduced perceived dyspnea during inspiratory resistive loading. A small COPD exercise study reported lower exertional dyspnea as a secondary outcome, not a primary dyspnea treatment result.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Respiratory system > Dyspnea category contains one human experimental study in healthy adults. One adjacent COPD exercise report also recorded exertional dyspnea, giving two relevant titles, but it is not a dedicated patient dyspnea trial. There are no direct case series or trials enrolling patients because dyspnea was their primary indication.

Human and clinical evidence

Izukura et al. studied 28 healthy adults exposed to inspiratory resistive loads. Phototherapy applied around the stellate-ganglion area reduced perceived dyspnea during the laboratory challenge (2019). A small randomized COPD study combining super-pulsed laser and LEDs reported lower exertional dyspnea during an exercise-performance protocol, alongside muscle-strength and fatigue outcomes (Miranda et al. 2015). That result is secondary to the trial's exercise focus and does not establish treatment for persistent breathlessness.

Animal evidence

No animal experiment is listed in the exact dyspnea category or in the single mapped COPD report.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study is listed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The healthy-volunteer study used linearly polarized phototherapy near the stellate-ganglion region during experimentally increased breathing resistance. The COPD study used combined laser and LED light before exercise. These are different interventions and settings. Wavelength describes the light's color band and influences tissue penetration; the protocols cannot be pooled as one treatment.

Interpretation

The laboratory result concerns perceived sensation during a controlled challenge, not day-to-day symptoms or disease outcomes. Evidence for people treated primarily for dyspnea remains very limited. A clinical trial should enroll patients with persistent breathlessness and measure activity, symptom burden, and adverse effects.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reducing experimentally induced dyspnea in healthy adults Very low for patient dyspnea because the COPD study measured it only as a secondary exercise symptom
Publications and records2 titles (one exact healthy-volunteer study plus one mapped COPD exercise report measuring dyspnea secondarily)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The exact indication has one healthy-volunteer experiment, and the mapped COPD report measured exertional dyspnea during a muscle-performance test. Neither tests a population receiving treatment primarily for breathlessness. A sham-controlled patient trial should use validated dyspnea scales and daily-function outcomes.
